title: Anti-Sicilian For White
description: A sneaky variation against the Najdorf and Dragon Sicilians (2...d6). We play 3.Nc3 and trick Black into our system with a central strike.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/2N5/2NP2P1/.text:
Black goes ...a6, controlling the b5 square.

Ideally, Black wants to play ...Bd7 and advance their b-pawn, but we won't allow them to achieve that.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/P1N5/2NP2P1.text:
We push our a-pawn, controlling b5 and looking to advance a5 in order to freeze Black's queenside.

Our position is great and we'll look to proceed by developing our dark-squared bishop to either e3 or f4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PP.text:
Black develops their other knight.

I suggest we go d3, preparing to develop our bishop to e3 or f4.

Trading on c6 was also possible but I really like the g2-bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppb2ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/2N5/1PN3P1/P.text:
And now we go b3, preparing to develop our dark-squared bishop.

We've got a powerful light-squared bishop and a pleasant position that's relatively easy to play.

Our c1-bishop can develop to either b2 or a3. It's also often useful to push the a-pawn in order to further stop Black from ever going ...b5.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
Black usually castles their king.

We'll also castle.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
Black can also castle and give us the option to capture the bishop.

This is played 15% of the time.

Trading our well placed knight for Black's bishop isn't all that great.

Instead, I suggest that we proceed by fianchettoing our bishop.

We'll castle our king and can then either fianchetto our dark-squared bishop, or develop it via d3 and Be3.

rnbq1rk1/ppb2ppp/4pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
Black usually castles their king.

We'll also castle.

Black's second option is to slide the bishop back to the e7-square.

We'll fianchetto, preparing to castle.

Our move of interest in this study is the natural ...Bd6, developing the bishop and attacking our knight.

This is played half the time.

Against this, we'll move our knight back to c4 and target Black's bishop.

rnbqk2r/ppb2ppp/4pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PPPP1.text:
The most common way to proceed is to slide the bishop back to c7.

This is played 50% of the time.

Now we'll fianchetto our bishop.

This bishop is really annoying for Black since it prevents them from easily developing the light-squared bishop or advancing the b-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
The main way for Black to proceed is to develop their kingside knight.

It's played 40% of the time, in almost 5 million games in the database.

The idea is to get us to advance our d-pawn and transpose back into normal lines.

But we'll advance our e-pawn!

This is an extremely rare and dangerous approach.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p1p3/8/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
Black captures the e-pawn.

We'll recapture with our knight.

Now our knight is active in the center and covering some key squares in Black's position.

This chapter will deal with 5...e6, the most common continuation.

This is played 30% of the time.

Black is simply preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop.

Against ...e6, we'll go for g3.

Our plan here is to fianchetto the light-squared bishop and castle kingside.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the Sicilian.

We'll develop our kingside knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black plays ...d6, controlling e5 and opening the light-squared bishop.

This move usually leads to various ultra-theoretical Sicilians such as the Najdorf or the Dragon, but we have a way to avoid these lines.

Instead of the typical d4, we are going to develop our other knight.

In this course, we'll learn a Two Knights Anti-Sicilian which deals specifically with ...d6 Sicilian setups.

And we develop our dark-squared bishop, attacking the rook again.

Black develops their light-squared bishop and offers a bishop trade.

Black recaptures with their pawn.

Black advances with ...b5.

Black goes ...b6, looking to develop their light-squared bishop to b7.

The most common way for Black to proceed is ...Rb8, preparing ...b5.

Black recaptures.

And we finish the sequence by bringing our rook down to a8.

Black is in trouble here. Our pieces are very active and it's really not easy for Black to make moves.

Black's queen is overworked, so the immediate threat here is Rxc8.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbppp/p3pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PP.text:
Black's third option is ...a6.

This is played 16% of the time.

Black's plan here is to go ...Rb8 and follow up by advancing ...b5.

Against ...a6, we'll push our a-pawn to control the b5-square.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4pn2/2p1N3/8/2N3P1/PPP.text:
The most logical way for Black to proceed is to develop their knight to d7 and propose a knight trade.

It wouldn't be great for us to just trade off our active knight, so we'll respond by jumping it back to c4.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PPP.text: And we also castle, transposing into the main line of this study.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/1n2pn2/2p5/2N5/2N3P1/PP.text:
Black's second option is to insist on trading the knights with ...Nb6.

This is played 31% of the time.

We should respond with b3, supporting the c4-knight and freeing up the b2-square for our other bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2p5/2P5/2N3P1/P1PP.text:
And we recapture.

Our pawns are doubled, but they aren't weak and the pawn on c4 covers the important d5-square.

Our plan here is to play d3 and develop the dark-squared bishop. 

We should also look to bring our rook to the semi-open b-file.

Against this, we can simply fianchetto our other bishop.

Black goes ...Be7, preparing ...O-O.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2p1N3/8/2N3P1/PPP.text:
Instead of ...Be7 or ...Bd6, Black can develop their other knight.

This, however, quickly transposes.

We don't want to trade our active knight, so we'll bring it back to c4.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2p1N3/8/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
Black usually castles their king.

We'll also castle our king.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/4pn2/2p1N3/8/2N3P1/PPPP1.text:
This study will deal with another option on move six, ...Be7.

This is played 25% of the time.

The bishop is less active here, but Black's idea is that we can't gain a tempo on the bishop.

We'll fianchetto our bishop.

As we saw previously, the bishop is a key asset since it makes it difficult for Black to move the b-pawn or develop the c8-bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black proceeds in the most natural way by developing the g8-knight.

And now we'll push our e-pawn!

This rare pawn advance is the signature idea of our Anti-Sicilian.

Black captures the e-pawn.

We'll recapture with our knight.

This pawn trade has allowed us to get an active knight in the center.

Black's most common continuation is ...e6, opening up the f8-bishop.

Black goes for the Sicilian.

Black plays ...d6, controlling e5 and opening the light-squared bishop.

Black castles as well.

Our rook is pinning the knight on the d-file, and we want to play Bb5 to add an attacker to it.

Too much to deal with.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/6p1/6B1/3Q4/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
Black has to recapture with the knight.

Anything else would lose material.

Now our queen is under attack, but we wanted to move it anyway.

We simply slide to c4 and there's some tension among the pieces.

Sure, they will develop and defend, probably thinking there's no danger.

Once they do that, we can bring the knight to c4.

White is much better.

The move ...a6 is only played 5% of the time, and it's an inaccuracy.

They could play ...a6 here, covering the b5-square.

We'll line up the bishop with the queen.

7...g6 might seem like a logical move, and it's played 14% of the time.

Black wants to develop the bishop on the dangerous diagonal and threaten our pieces that way.

However, it's a mistake because it removes one of the defenders of the f6-knight, and we'll take advantage of that by attacking it.

Things could get messy for Black soon.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/2p1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
This chapter will deal with 5...Nd7. We have already covered 5...e6 in Chapter 1.

5...Nd7 is a way for Black to try and trade off our active knight immediately.

It's played 20% of the time, in just over 30,000 games.

We won't capture. Instead, I suggest d4!

This is a great way to defend the knight and bring another piece to the game quickly.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/4N3/3p4/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
You will most likely see Black capture on d4 here.

And we'll take back with the queen, defending the knight.

We've already got three pieces out and two of them are in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/4Q3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
This move doesn't work at all.

It's a huge blunder that immediately loses for Black.

So, look out for this because it seems natural and I expect a lot of players to play it.

Now Bb5+ wins, as you will see.

Our idea is to pin one of Black's pieces, and then develop and attack its defenders.

It might even be the best move for the Black king to get out of the way.

So Black captures it.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/6p1/4Q1B1/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text: The knight recaptures, but it's pinned to the queen now.

They can recapture with the knight and it seems like some trades are incoming.

Of course, Black plays ...Bg7 to defend.

This pins Black's bishop and completely restricts their position.

Black blocks with the bishop.

Black is already in trouble.

Black will most likely block with the bishop.

2k2b1r/1p1rp1pp/p3p3/2p5/P5n1/2N5/1PP1KP.text: Once the rook recaptures, here's another point of a4.

2k2b1r/1p1rp1pp/p3p3/P1p5/6n1/2N5/1PP1KP.text:
We can play a5 and take aim at the weaknesses in Black's position.

We just locked down the queenside so they can't protect the c5-pawn.

Apart from that, the b6-square is an outpost for our knight and the e-pawns are still extremely weak.

We'll kick out the knight with h3, play Be3 to attack c5, and go Na4 to threaten Nb6+ with a fork.

2kr1b1r/1p1bp1pp/p3p3/1Bp5/P5n1/2N5/1PP1.text:
Black won't bite.

They force us to make a decision instead.

We'll take on d7.

2kr1b1r/1p2p1pp/p3p3/2p5/6n1/2N5/PPP1KPP.text:
Black now wins a pawn by capturing on e6, albeit the extra pawn resulting is rather sickly.

We aren't done venturing with the knight.

2kr1b1r/1p2p1pp/p3p3/2p5/N5n1/8/PPP1KPPP.text:
We'll jump to a4 with the idea of attacking the c5-pawn, as well as jumping to the b6-square if needed.

We'll add an attacker on the pawn in the form of Be3.

Of course, we can kick out the knight with h3 at some point.

Black has probably played in the most resilient way, but White is still slightly better.

2kr1b1r/1p2pppp/p3P3/1Np5/6n1/8/PPP1KPPP.text:
Black tries to force back our active knight.

We'll simply retreat to c3.

2kr1b1r/pp1bp1pp/4p3/1Bp5/6n1/2N5/PPP1KP.text:
A logical move is to castle here.

Black activates the a-rook instead of taking our bishop.

We'll protect the bishop with a4 now.

We would love to open up the a-file for our rook.

2kr1b1r/pp2pppp/4P3/1Np5/6n1/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The best move is for Black to castle.

This is with check and avoids the fork.

We'll slide to e2.

Black can capture on e6 now.

N2k1b1r/pp2p1pp/4p3/2p5/5B2/8/PPP1K1PP/R.text:
This means that our knight will be able to get out, while Black's won't.

We will be up a piece and completely winning.

Courtesy of 10.e6.

N2k1b1r/pp2p1pp/4p3/2p5/8/8/PPP1K1PP/R1B.text:
Now Black takes on e6.

But the whole reason behind our position being winning is that they can't open up their dark-squared bishop now, while ours is free to roam the board.

r1b1kb1r/pp1npppp/8/2p1P3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
Retreating to d7 is the more passive option, but not a huge mistake.

Black is attacking the e5-pawn.

We have bigger fish to fry.

We'll jump into the center and threaten a fork.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p1P3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
A trade of queens will most likely ensue.

We'll take back with the king to keep our knight on c3 active.

Castling isn't as important here as there isn't much danger to our king.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/8/2p1P3/6n1/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
The more aggressive option for Black is 8...Ng4.

It looks dangerous because Black is attacking both the e5- and the f2-pawns and threatening a fork.

That's why it's important to know the theory here.

We'll give a check first.

r1bk1b1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2pNP1B1/8/8/PPP2PP.text:
But we have this check.

Black can neither go to e8 because of the fork, nor block with the bishop on e7.

They will most likely have to play ...f6 and lose a pawn at some point.

White is slightly better.

r1bk1b1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2pNP3/5B2/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black can even make an inaccuracy easily in this line.

10...e6 seems natural to attack the knight and open up the bishop.

r1bk1b1r/pp1npppp/8/2pNP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
Black plays the only reasonable defensive move.

Let's develop and protect the e5-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2b5/2Q2B2/2N5/PPP2.text:
And we will castle long now.

The knight on d7 is pinned and under attack, and it is the only defender of the bishop on c5.

White is slightly better.

The knight recaptures.

Black has to continue protecting the c5-bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2b1N3/2Q2B2/2N5/P.text:
Black castles and gets their king into safety.

First of all, we'll capture on d7.

This trade is good because it makes our upcoming threat harder to defend.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2b1B3/8/2N2Q2/PPP2P.text: Black castles, and we can finish our kingside development now.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2b1B3/8/2NB1Q2/PPP2.text:
We've suddenly got both bishops eyeing the kingside, with an active queen to help them.

We are actually flexible on where we want to castle in this line, as our position is comfortable either way.

There might be more pressure coming soon.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2b1N3/3Q1B2/2N5/PP.text:
Black's idea is that they can develop to c5 with tempo on our queen.

We'll keep the queen close, though.

Continuing to apply pressure is best.

Black's pieces are solid for now, but we are aiming to castle queenside.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2b1N3/5B2/2N5/PPP2.text:
Taking with the bishop loses a tempo considering Black had just played ...Be7.

Let's develop the queen and get it away from the d-file.

The f3-square is probably best.

We open up the d-file for our rook.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/4pn2/2p1N3/3P1B2/2N5/PP.text:
Black continues in a solid but passive manner. They want to castle and get out of trouble.

We won't make it that easy.

I suggest we take on c5.

Black has to recapture with one of the pieces, and it's better to recapture with the bishop.

Recapturing with the knight allows a queen trade and that gives us the advantage.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2b1n3/5B2/2N2Q2/PPP2.text:
Black will capture on e5 at some point.

That's why we need the bishop on f4.

We'll recapture.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2p1N3/3P4/2N5/PPP.text:
They can open up the dark-squared bishop quickly and look to castle.

This is played 11% of the time.

We'll activate the dark-squared bishop and provide more protection to the knight on e5. 

It helps to develop it quickly because we will castle queenside in some lines.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/4N3/3p1B2/2N5/PPP.text:
Black can choose to capture on d4 now.

This changes things a bit because their dark-squared bishop is already open.

We'll recapture.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/2p1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
As mentioned, 5...Nbd7 is the topic of this chapter.

We'll defend the knight with d4, as seen in the 6...cxd4 study.

However, in this study we will take a look at some alternatives to Black capturing in the center on move 6.

It's not necessary for them to activate our queen in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p1n3/3P4/2N5/PPP2P.text:
What if Black decides to make some trades here?

This is definitely a variation we have to explore because a lot of players look to trade when they find themselves in unknown theoretical positions.

We'll recapture, of course.

r2k1b1r/ppN1pppp/4P3/2p5/8/8/PPP1K1PP/R1.text:
Black slides to d8...

And we'll take the rook in the corner.

r3kb1r/1p1bp1pp/p3p3/1Bp5/6n1/2N5/PPP1KP.text:
They could attack our bishop here.

There's no point in retreating now.

We'll capture on d7.

r3kb1r/pp1bp1pp/4p3/1Bp5/6n1/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
Black can definitely capture with the pawn, but now the e-pawns are doubled, isolated and weak.

This is much better for us than them being able to capture on e5 with the knight.

Let's defend against the fork on f2.

It's not in Black's interests to capture on b5 and face more threats.

r3kb1r/pp1bpppp/8/1Bp1P3/6n1/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
Black blocks with the bishop.

And here's a very important move: we'll push e6!

This seems completely counter-intuitive, however our e5-pawn was already under attack and now we are threatening the pinned bishop.

Also, we are shutting down their dark-squared bishop completely, which will prove to be crucial in one line.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/4P3/1Np5/8/8/PPP1K1PP/R1B.text:
Black will take the rook, of course.

But we also have a fork with Nc7+.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/4P3/1Np5/8/8/PPP2nPP/R1BK.text:
Black can choose to capture on f2.

But that's a losing blunder.

We'll move to e2 and attack the knight.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/4P3/1bp5/6n1/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
Capturing on b5 is a viable option, but it allows more threats from us.

We'll recapture with the knight.

We are letting Black fork us on f2, but we are threatening a fork ourselves.

That's why we didn't capture on f7 first. We prefer the Black king to be on e8.

r4b1r/1p1kp1pp/p3p3/2p5/6n1/2N5/PPP1KPPP.text:
The king recaptures.

And now we will jump to e4.

This is a great move because it not only attacks the c5-pawn, but also has a hidden point to it.

r4b1r/1p2p1pp/p1k1p3/2p3N1/6n1/8/PPP1KPP.text:
We can jump to g5 and attack Black's weak structure!

It's not convenient for Black to move the king back to the d-file.

In fact, the best move is probably ...h6, allowing us to capture on e6.

White is slightly better.

r4b1r/1p2p1pp/p1k1p3/2p5/4N1n1/8/PPP1KPP.text: The idea is that once Black defends...

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black continues with ...Nf6, probably not ready for what's about to come.

And that's e5, of course.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black plays the Sicilian Defense.

We'll continue with the natural Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black plays the standard d6.

We'll activate the second knight as well.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
More 5...Nbd7 setups can include a trade of knights on move 6 and the simple 6...e6. 

Let's see how these middlegames often turn out.

We'll begin with 1.e4.

r1bqk2r/p3bppp/2p1pn2/2p5/2B5/1PN5/P1PP1.text:
Instead of playing d3 and developing it that way, I suggest we fianchetto.

This will take more control of the long diagonal and especially the e5-square, since we don't want Black to push ...e5.

Our queen will join the game via Qf3 and target the c6-pawn.

White is better.

r1bqk2r/p3bppp/2p1pn2/2p5/2B5/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
The bishop comes out, and Black is ready to castle too.

And here's a good plan for our dark-squared bishop.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1pbp/4pnp1/1Bp1N3/8/2N2Q2/PP.text:
The best move is to block with the b-knight.

We'll capture, as was our idea when we played Bb5+.

r1bqkb1r/p3pppp/2p2n2/2p5/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
The b-pawn has to take back, and look at the pawn structure now.

Doubled, isolated c-pawns.

We've already achieved a positional victory and we can simply develop and castle.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/2p5/2B5/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
Black opens up their dark-squared bishop...

But we will castle quickly.

Standard stuff.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2p1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1.text:
Black can offer a trade of knights on the c6-square.

This is different to 5...Nbd7 because here we have the opportunity to weaken Black's pawns.

This inaccuracy is played 11% of the time.

We'll capture.

r2q1rk1/pQ1b1pbp/4pnp1/2p1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1.text: Black castles to get into safety...

And so will we.

White has won a pawn with no clear compensation for Black, so there is no debate about who is better.

r2qk2r/pp1b1pbp/4pnp1/2p1N3/8/2N2Q2/PPPP.text:
Black has to recapture with the bishop.

But that leaves the b7-pawn hanging.

Basically, this means that Black lost a pawn by force, thanks to our fast development and the Bb5+ move.

rn1qk2r/p4Qbp/4pnp1/1bp1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
And that's checkmate.

A win in 10 moves. Not bad.

rn1qk2r/pQ3pbp/4pnp1/1bp1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1P.text: If Black captures on b5, there is something even better.

rn1qk2r/pp1b1pbp/4pnp1/1Bp1N3/8/2N2Q2/PP.text:
If they instead block with the bishop the game is over.

We'll just take on b7 and attack the rook.

rnbqk2r/pp3pbp/4pnp1/2p1N3/2B5/2N2Q2/PPP.text:
Now they have time to fianchetto, because there is no immediate danger.

And here I suggest an unorthodox-looking move.

It's to play with the bishop again and give a check.

This forces Black to block with one of their pieces and they have to be accurate in order to defend.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/2p1N3/8/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
The move ...g6 is played 13% of the time or in just over 20,000 games.

It's not optimal because it gives us an easy line of attack.

And that's to activate the bishop and target the f7-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black develops on f6.

And now our trademark e5.

We attack the knight and give Black a choice.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p1p3/8/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
They'll most likely capture.

And we will take back.

Now Black has a couple of options as sidelines.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/4pnp1/2p1N3/2B5/2N5/PPPP.text:
Black pushes ...e6, blocking.

But our attack is not over.

The queen comes out to f3 and pressures other weak spots!

In the span of just a few moves, we've developed most of the pieces and are already targeting Black's weaknesses.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the Sicilian.

We'll develop the king's knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black connects their pawns.

We'll activate our knights first.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we'll learn to play against Dragon-like setups with 5...g6 and against Black playing two knights forward with 5...Nc6.

Let's start with e4.

1r1k3r/1B1b1R1p/p2p1p2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1P.text: Sure, Black can take the bishop...

1r1k3r/1B1bRppp/p2p1B2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1P.text:
Black has to move to d8 not to lose the bishop on d7.

But we will simply capture on f7 with check.

1r1k3r/3b1R1p/B2p1p2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1P/2.text:
But we will take on a6 as well and in this line we are winning because of the material advantage.

Even though we are down an exchange, we are up three pawns and who is going to stop them?

Besides, Black's pawns are extremely weak.

1r2k2r/1B1bbppp/p2p1B2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1P.text:
Blocking with the bishop on e7 doesn't result in checkmate immediately but it is desperate.

We'll take with the rook.

1r2kb1r/1B1b1ppp/p2p1B2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1.text:
Black attacks the bishop, but we have an intermezzo.

And that's the check on e1.

Black has two options.

1r2kb1r/1B3ppp/p2pbB2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1P/.text: If Black blocks with the bishop on e6, then we see why capturing on b7 came before Re1+.

r1b1kb1r/1p1npppp/p7/3N2B1/3Q4/6P1/PPP2P.text:
But we will just make another threat with Nd5.

This is way too much for Black to deal with.

r1b1kb1r/1p1npppp/p7/6B1/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2P.text: They can try to hold and defend against both threats with ...Nd7.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p1q2n2/8/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
Black will most likely recapture with the queen and attack our rook.

But I suggest an incredible move to remember.

It's Bg5!

Sacrificing the rook, we develop and attack the knight on f6.

What's the idea?

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/2p1P3/8/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
Black can even trade the queens.

After this, we will recapture with the knight and preserve castling rights.

We also want to keep protecting the f2-square.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/6B1/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
Well, if Black takes the rook...

We will castle long!

If you know you should play 10.Bg5, you have to understand why, and this is it.

Suddenly, we are threatening to checkmate on d8 as well as to check on b5 with a discovered attack on the queen.

White is winning.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p7/2p1P3/5Pn1/6P1/PPP4P.text:
The f4-push protects the e5-pawn and we create a nice and stable pawn chain.

Behind it, we will activate the light-squared bishop.

White is slightly better already.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p7/2p1P3/6n1/6P1/PPP2P1.text: With f2 protected, the knight moving to g4 doesn't achieve anything.

r1b1kb1r/1pq1pppp/p1n2n2/4N3/3Q4/2N3P1/P.text:
Once the knight arrives on c6, we don't have many options.

We have to trade on c6.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p4n2/2p1N3/8/2N3P1/PPP.text:
A move that's played 24% of the time is ...Nbd7.

Black offers a trade of knights this way, but we have already seen a similar position.

Our go-to move is d4 to expand and protect the knight.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p4n2/4N3/3p4/2N3P1/PPP.text:
The most natural move is to take the pawn here.

But we should already be familar with a position like this.

We'll take with the queen, protecting the knight.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/2p1n3/3P4/2N3P1/PP.text:
Sure, Black can trade here.

But they won't get much out of it.

We'll take and hit the f6-knight.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/4n3/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
The knight captures on e5.

We'll simply take back.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/4Q3/5B2/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
We can get the bishop to f4 and prevent Black from activating to the most optimal square.

Next, we will simply fianchetto and castle.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/4Q3/8/2N3P1/PPP2P1.text: And once a move like ...e6 arrives...

r1q1kb1r/1p1bpppp/p4B2/8/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2P.text:
If they move to c8, we will explain how White is winning in a bit more depth than the 10...Bd7 line.

We'll take on g7 and attack the rook.

It doesn't make much sense for Black to capture on g7 as our queen would invade and it would be even tougher to defend.

r1q1kbr1/1p1bppBp/p7/8/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2PBP.text:
So they will probably slide to g8.

After which we can take the bishop.

r1q1kr2/1p1bpp1p/p7/3N4/3Q4/6P1/PPP2PBP/.text:
We've got this Nd5 move and we are getting in.

The knight is threatening to jump to b6, and there are ideas of placing a piece on the e-file and threatening Nf6 if Black defends with something like ...Qd8.

We're completely winning even though down an exchange.

r1q1kr2/1p1bpp1p/p7/8/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2PBP/.text: The idea is that once the rook recaptures...

r3kb1r/1p1b1ppp/p2p1B2/8/8/2N3P1/PPP2PBP.text:
They recapture.

And we will take on b7 now, attacking the rook.

Soon the bishop will be able to give check on c6, which will prove to be very strong.

Similar to the 10...Bd7 line.

r3kb1r/1p1bpppp/p1q2B2/8/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2P.text:
And the beautiful thing is, if Black retreats to c6 to defend...

We can sacrifice the f1-bishop!

This is a common deflection tactic and transposes to the main line of this study.

Black can't take because of checkmate.

r3kb1r/1p1bpppp/p1q2n2/6B1/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP.text:
Black could try to place the bishop on d7 and block our queen's vision.

Also, the bishop covers any potential Bb5+ ideas.

But that loses the game.

We will castle here.

Now both the queen and the rook attack the vulnerable bishop on d7.

r3kb1r/1p1bpppp/p2q1B2/8/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2P.text:
They will probably slide to d6 and offer a trade.

But we don't mind.

Capturing on d6 is winning, too.

r3kb1r/1p1bpppp/p4n2/6B1/3Q4/2N3P1/PPP2P.text:
And if Black takes the rook in the corner...

The attack on d7 becomes even stronger when we remove that bishop's defender.

Now they can't afford to recapture our bishop.

The best move is to block with ...Bd7.

But that is basically giving up a piece.

Because we can remove the bishop's defender with Bxf6 and threaten to capture it.

r3kb1r/1p2pppp/p1q2B2/8/3Q2b1/2N3P1/PPP2.text: We'll take on f6. Black's best response here is the unfathomable 11...h5!! (preventing Qxg4) and even after this we'll keep up the pressure with 12.Nd5. Black will have a hard time defending.

r3kb1r/1p2pppp/p1q2n2/6B1/3Q2b1/2N3P1/PP.text:
The best move for Black is actually ...Bg4.

The bishop is preventing us from castling and Black awaits our response.

rnb1k2r/1p3ppp/p1q1pn2/2b5/2N2Q2/2N3P1/P.text:
And if they don't, our queen is still active on f4.

Our rook on h1 is now under attack.

We'll simply slide it to g1.

We've got a lot of ideas incoming, like Bg2 to hit the queen again, as well as Be3 to trade the dark-squared bishops.

Black's bishop on c8 is still passive.

We'll castle queenside, with an advantage.

rnb1k2r/1pq2ppp/p3pn2/2b5/2NQ4/2N3P1/PPP.text:
If Black plays ...Bc5.

But we will simply offer a trade on f4.

If Black takes, our bishop will get developed actively.

rnb1kb1r/1pq1pppp/p4n2/2p1N3/8/2N3P1/PPP.text:
A move that is played 19% of the time is ...Qc7, attacking the knight.

Black's queen is safe and posing problems.

We don't want to move the knight. We will push d4 instead.

Our idea is not only to protect the knight, but to play Bf4 and target the queen.

rnb1kb1r/1pq1pppp/p4n2/4N3/3p4/2N3P1/PPP.text:
Black takes.

And we will recapture.

rnb1kb1r/1pq2ppp/p3pn2/2p1N3/3P4/2N3P1/P.text:
Black could play ...e6 here.

The idea is to meet our potential Bf4 with ...Bd6.

We will retreat to c4 instead.

And so will we.

r1b1k2r/1p2bppp/p1nppq2/8/4P3/2PQ1N2/PP3.text:
We don't need to rush with Bg5 if Black goes to e7.

Simple development will suffice.

Let's activate the light-squared bishop first.

r1b1kb1r/1p3pp1/p1nppq1p/8/4P3/2PQ1N2/PP.text:
Black prevents Bg5 with this logical move.

So we will just continue developing.

The e2-square is fine for the bishop as it covers g4 from there.

And you will see our plan soon.

r1b1kb1r/1p3ppp/p1nppq2/8/4P3/3Q1N2/PPP2.text:
The queen recaptures, and now we would love to activate the dark-squared bishop, but the b2-pawn would be hanging.

So c3 makes sense.

We are now aiming to eventually play against the d6-weakness.

r1b2rk1/1p2bpp1/p1nppq1p/8/4P1P1/2PQBN2/.text:
In the form of g4.

Since the queen is on f6, it's an excellent target for g5.

If the g-file opens, we will be in good shape.

On the other hand, we will castle queenside to bring the king to safety.

r1b2rk1/1p2bpp1/p1nppq1p/8/4P3/2PQBN2/PP.text: But after Black castles, I suggest an immediate pawn advance...

r1b2rk1/1p2bppp/p1nppq2/8/4P3/2PQBN2/PP2.text:
We will do the same with the dark-squared bishop.

We could choose to castle queenside and have a sharp battle trying to push the pawns on opposite sides.

But we could also castle short and play more of a positional game.

White is slightly better, but nothing substantial yet.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/3p4/p2P4/1n6/1Q3N2/PPP2.text:
Black can maintain the knight, but only for one move.

We will kick it out immediately with a3.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/n2p4/p2P4/8/PQ2BN2/1PP2.text:
We'll activate the bishop to e3 and cover the c5-square.

Our pieces are active and we'll probably castle queenside.

White is winning!

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/n2p4/p2P4/8/PQ3N2/1PP2P.text:
Black retreats the knight to a6.

They might want to bring it to c5.

So let's develop accordingly.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1np1n2/8/4P3/2NQ1N2/PP.text:
Black continues developing.

And we'll offer a knight trade here.

This might help us grab space and improve the mobility of our pieces.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1np4/3n4/4P3/3Q1N2/PPP.text:
Black capturing works out great for us.

We'll take back with the pawn and hit the knight.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p4/3P4/1n6/3Q1N2/PPP2.text:
If it jumps to b4, we can simply slide to the queenside as mentioned.

Nb4 is not a good move.

From b3, our queen attacks the knight and takes aim at b7.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p4/3Pn3/8/3Q1N2/PPP2P.text:
Black jumps into the center.

It's definitely advantageous for us to trade here.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p7/3Pp3/8/1Q6/PPP2PPP/R.text:
We can go ahead with the Qb3 idea.

The queen eyes the b7-pawn in case Black develops the c8-bishop.

We'll enhance that threat with the Be2-Bf3 maneuver.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1nppn2/3N4/4P3/3Q1N2/PP.text:
Black doesn't have to trade and let us get what we want.

Instead, they can force our hand.

But we are ready for that too.

Let's take the knight on f6.

The idea is that we induced Black to weaken their structure by playing both ...d6 and ...e6 and now the d6-pawn will be weak.

r1bqkb1r/5ppp/p1pppn2/4P3/3Q4/1PN2N2/P1P.text:
To push e5!

With the similar idea as in any other e5-line in this course, we want to attack the knight and potentially split Black's pawns.

White is slightly better, but Black can probably equalize with perfect play.

r1bqkb1r/5ppp/p1pppn2/8/3QP3/1PN2N2/P1P2.text: Black can try to place the knight on f6, but as soon as they do that, remember...

r1bqkbnr/1p2pppp/p1np4/8/3QP3/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
Instead, expect Black to attack the queen right away.

We won't retreat all the way to d1 but rather to d3.

This helps our queen stay somewhat active.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1npp3/1B6/3QP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Attacking the bishop now doesn't make much of a difference in our approach.

We have to capture.

r1bqkbnr/5ppp/p1ppp3/8/3QP3/2N2N2/PPP2PP.text:
The b-pawn recaptures and now Black has three pawns on the sixth rank which do restrict our knights.

However, they also restrict Black's own bishops.

All in all, we have three developed pieces so far against Black's none.

And with b3, we'll aim to develop a fourth one.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/8/3QP3/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
Since we can pin the Black knight once it arrives on c6.

We will play Bb5. This way our queen can stay in the center for longer and allow for active central play.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2np1n2/1B2p1B1/4P3/2NQ1.text:
We can simply slide to g5 and pin the knight.

Now there is a big hole on the d5-square which we will definitely use.

If Black doesn't react, we can even place the knight on d5 on the next move.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4PB2/2NQ1N.text:
Which is why Black will probably have to push ...e5 to save the pawn.

But that has its disadvantages, of course.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2nppn2/1B6/4P3/2NQ1N2/P.text:
Black can develop all they want, but we have our plan.

After Bf4, the pawn is attacked twice.

And if needed, we can bring the rook to d1 to attack it the third time.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/2npp3/1B6/3QP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
If Black chooses to unpin here, we don't have to rush and capture the knight right away.

Simply sliding to d3 is good because we keep an attack on the d6-pawn and look to place the bishop on f4 to add an attacker.

rnbqkbnr/1p2pppp/p2p4/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Black could play ...a6 already on move 3 to take away the b5-square from our pieces.

But that wastes a precious tempo and gives us time to expand in the center.

This move is only played 8% of the time.

Let's go for d4.

rnbqkbnr/1p2pppp/p2p4/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
After Black captures, it might seem like we want a standard Sicilian by recapturing with the knight.

But we will actually take with the queen!

This will definitely spice things up.

If Black allows it to remain active, we've already seen what the queen can do in previous chapters.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black plays the Sicilian.

We'll develop the king's knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black goes for ...d6.

Our two knights are now out.

Let's look at some other third move deviations.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/3pp3/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
The move ...e6 might be designed to try and prepare ...d5, although that looks risky.

Otherwise, maybe Black just wants to stay solid and play a small center game. This is played in 10% of games.

In some cases, the d6-pawn could be a target when they play ...e6 like this, however.

Either way, it gives us space and time to push d4.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/3pp3/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black takes.

And we'll recapture with the queen!

Since Black hasn't played ...a6, taking with the queen here might prove to be powerful.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The moves 3...e6 and 3...a6 can be played very early on. 

We'll break in the center with d4 against both of them.

Let's take a look at these lines, starting with our 1.e4.

r1b1kb1r/p3pp1p/2p2np1/4N3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
Don't rush with capturing on c6 if Black slides to e8.

If we take now, there is ...Bb7 with a skewer.

r1b1kb1r/p3pp1p/2p2np1/4N3/8/2N5/PPPB1PP.text: We can just develop and prepare to castle on the next move. c6 remains a permanent weakness for Black.

r1bk1b1r/p3pp1p/2p2np1/4p3/8/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
The pawn recaptures.

And now there is an even bigger threat after we capture on e5.

We are threatening both a fork and the pawn on c6.

r1bk1b1r/pp2pp1p/2n2np1/1B2p3/8/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black has to recapture with the king.

Now the knight is not pinned anymore and is actually protecting the e5-pawn.

So we will take it as well.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n2np1/1B2p3/3Q4/2N2N2/.text:
If Black captures on e5 now, our plans don't change much compared to the 6...dxe5 line.

We will trade the queens first.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2np1np1/4P3/3Q4/2N2N2/P.text:
Black can for an intermezzo here, forking our queen and the pawn on e5.

But we will simply pin the knight with Bb5 and neutralize it.

r2k1b1r/p3pp1p/2p1bnp1/4N3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
If Black commits the bishop to e6...

We can actually capture on c6 with check and there is no ...Bb7 to cause any trouble.

Black has made a mistake with their last move.

r4b1r/p1k1pp1p/2N1bnp1/8/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text: The king slides to c7 to attack the knight.

r4b1r/p1k1pp1p/4bnp1/8/3N4/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
But we can retreat to d4 and hit the bishop.

We've won a clean pawn and Black's position is a mess.

Black allowing us to capture on e6 would be horrible for their pawn structure.

White is winning.

rn1k1b1r/pp2pp1p/4bnp1/4N3/8/2N1B3/PPP2P.text:
But we have the momentum and we'll simply continue development.

We can castle long with check on the next move and claim a positional as well as an activity advantage.

White is much better here.

rn1k1b1r/pp2pp1p/4bnp1/4N3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text: They can defend against the threat with the bishop.

rnbk1b1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/4p3/8/2N2N2/PPP2PP.text:
The idea is that once the king captures...

We can take on e5 and threaten a fork.

Black has lost their castling rights and they still have to react to our knight.

rnbqk1nr/pp3pbp/3p2p1/4N3/3QP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
An attempt to trick us and pin the knight is for Black to fianchetto now.

But it doesn't work.

rnbqk1nr/pp3pbp/3p2p1/4N3/Q3P3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Because we can simply slide to a4 with check.

If Black blocks with the bishop, we will capture.

Otherwise we've just won an important central pawn and Black has no compensation for it.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3QP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
The most natural response is for Black to develop the knight, blocking our queen's vision, and prepare to fianchetto on the next move.

This is by far the most common move, played 72% of the time.

Let's continue in Anti-Sicilian style, and push e5 now that we see the knight on f6.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/4p3/3Q4/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
Capturing on e5 only gives us the advantage.

We'll trade queens.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the Sicilian.

We'll develop the knight to f3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
It's 3...g6.

Black can choose to fianchetto the bishop in basically any Sicilian variation, so this is something we have to cover here as well.

Our main antidote to this will be to immediately push d4 and try to get the queen to the center to counteract the bishop.

3...g6 is played just over 5% of the time, in more than 785,000 games.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
Black captures.

And we will take back with the queen, as mentioned.

Black still can't fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
And Black connects their pawns.

Let's get the other knight to c3 now.

We are now going to take a look at a specific variation Black can play.

rnbqkbnr/pp3p1p/3p2p1/4p3/3QP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Going for the quick ...e5 loses the game on the spot.

And it's played 10% of the time.

We can just sacrifice on e5!

rnbqkbnr/pp3p1p/6p1/4Q3/4P3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text: There's a fork and we'll simply win the rook.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Finally, let's take a look at 3...g6.

Here we'll play 4.d4 as well.

All of our pieces will thrive in this open position.

Let's start with 1.e4.
